rows.question: i have [[Hardened Scales]] and [[Doubling Season]] and cast ballista for X=2. how many counters does it come in with? do i get to pick the order or is it timestamps
rows.expected_answer: You choose the order and the best answer is 6. Walking Ballista's 'enters with X +1/+1 counters' is a replacement effect (614.1c, 614.12), and Hardened Scales and Doubling Season are further replacement effects modifying the same event. When multiple replacement effects apply to the same event, the affected permanent's controller picks which applies first (616.1), and since none of the special priorities in 616.1a-d apply, any may be chosen (616.1e). Each effect applies only once to the event (614.5). Apply Scales first (2 -> 3), then Season doubles (3 -> 6). Timestamps are irrelevant for replacement effects; that is the layer system for continuous effects.

outcome.answer: You choose. With **Walking Ballista** cast for X=2, it's trying to enter the battlefield with 2 +1/+1 counters, an event two replacement effects want to modify: **Hardened Scales** ("that many plus one" ) and **Doubling Season** ("twice that many"). Neither is a self-replacement effect, a control-changing effect, a copy effect, or a face-up/face-down effect, so under `616.1e` any applicable effect may be chosen first, and it's the affected permanent's controller (you) who picks the order, not timestamps (`616.1`). Order changes the result: apply Hardened Scales first (2→3), then Doubling Season doubles that (3→6); apply Doubling Season first (2→4), then Hardened Scales adds one (4→5). So you can choose to have **Walking Ballista** enter with as many as 6 +1/+1 counters by applying Hardened Scales before Doubling Season. This matches the ruling that when multiple effects modify how many counters are put on a creature you control, you choose the order.
citations: rule 616.1: "the affected object’s controller (or its owner if it has no controller) or the affected player chooses one to apply, following the steps listed below."
rule 616.1e: "Any of the applicable replacement and/or prevention effects may be chosen."

rule 616.1f: "Once the chosen effect has been applied, this process is repeated (taking into account only replacement or prevention effects that would now be applicable) until there are no more left to apply."

ruling a1f3da21-af6d-450e-bf0b-985d158418e6/636b245ed2960105: "If two or more effects attempt to modify how many counters would be put on a creature you control, you choose the order to apply those effects, no matter who controls the sources of those effects."

rows.expected_answer: Tron is off. Blood Moon is a type-changing effect (layer 4, 613.1d) that sets each nonbasic land's subtype to Mountain. Per 305.7, a land whose subtype is set to a basic land type loses its old land types (so it is no longer an Urza's land), loses all abilities from its rules text (the colorless mana ability), and gains only '{T}: Add {R}'. Each Urza's land is a plain Mountain that taps for one red mana; Tower does not produce three because it no longer has that ability and the others no longer have the Urza's subtype. They are still nonbasic (305.8), so Blood Moon keeps affecting them.

outcome.answer: N o - w it h B l ood Moon out none of your Tron lands can make their old mana at all. Blood Moon reads "Nonbasic lands are Mountains," which sets each land's subtype under `305.7`. That rule says the land "loses all abilities generated from its rules text, its old land types...and it gains the appropriate mana ability" for Mountain, i.e. `{T}: Add {R}`. So Urza's Tower, Urza's Mine and Urza's Power Plant all lose the Urza's Tower/Urza's Mine/Urza's Power-Plant land types and lose their own `{T}: Add {C}...` abilities entirely - they become plain (nonbasic) Mountains that just tap for {R}, per the Blood Moon ruling that nonbasic lands 'gain the land type Mountain and gain the ability "{T}: Add {R}".' There's no more conditional ability left to check land types with, so you can't get the {C}{C}{C} from Tower or any bonus from Mine/Power Plant - you just get one red mana per land, three total, not seven.

rows.question: ok classic one. I have [[Humility]] out and my opponent drops [[Opalescence]]. what are Humility and Opalescence now?? are all my creatures still 1/1? does the answer change if Opalescence was out first?
rows.expected_answer: Walk the layers. Opalescence reads 'each OTHER non-Aura enchantment', so it never affects itself: Opalescence stays a noncreature enchantment and keeps its ability in every scenario. Layer 4 (613.1d): Opalescence makes Humility a 'creature' enchantment. Layer 6 (613.1f): Humility removes all abilities from every creature, including itself; per 613.6 an effect that has started applying keeps applying in later layers even though its source ability is gone. Layer 7b (613.4b): Humility's 'base P/T 1/1' and Opalescence's 'base P/T equal to mana value' both set Humility's P/T. Neither depends on the other under 613.8a (applying one doesn't change the text, existence, or targets of the other), so timestamp order decides (613.7). If Opalescence has the later timestamp: Humility is a 4/4 creature with no abilities. If Humility has the later timestamp: Humility is a 1/1 creature with no abilities. Either way every ordinary creature is a 1/1 with no abilities, and Opalescence is an unaffected noncreature enchantment. Any other non-Aura enchantment Opalescence animates follows Humility itself: its base power and toughness are its mana value when Opalescence is later, and 1/1 when Humility is.

rows.question: quick one: if I have [[Valki, God of Lies]] in hand can I just cast the Tibalt side for 7? and while it's in my library/graveyard does it count as a planeswalker card for stuff like Vraska's Contempt / Kaya's Ghostform?
rows.expected_answer: Yes. Valki // Tibalt is a modal double-faced card: when you cast it you choose which face you're casting before it goes on the stack, and only that face is evaluated (712.11b, 712.11c), so you can cast Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor for {5}{B}{R} straight from your hand. Once chosen, the spell/permanent has only that face's characteristics (712.8f). But anywhere other than the stack or battlefield (hand, library, graveyard, exile) an MDFC has only its front face's characteristics (712.8a), so it is a legendary creature card named Valki, God of Lies there — never a planeswalker card.

outcome.answer:
Yes — **Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor** is a modal double-faced card, so when you cast it from hand you choose which face you're casting before it goes on the stack (per `712.11b`). If you choose the Tibalt side, you cast it for its printed cost, {5}{B}{R} (7 mana total, needing at least one black and one red source), and it resolves as **Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor**, a planeswalker, per `712.8f` ("While a modal double-faced spell is on the stack or a modal double-faced permanent is on the battlefield, it has only the characteristics of the face that's up").

But in your hand, library, or graveyard, it is *not* a planeswalker card — while a double-faced card is in any zone other than the battlefield or stack, it has only the characteristics of its front face (`712.8a`), which is Valki, a creature. So for anything checking card type while it's in the library or graveyard (mill/discard effects, reanimation targeting "planeswalker card," etc.), it only counts as a creature card, never a planeswalker card, until it's actually on the battlefield with the Tibalt face up.
citations: rule 712.11b: "A player casting a modal double-faced card or a copy of a modal double-faced card as a spell chooses which face they are casting before putting it onto the stack."
rule 712.8f: "While a modal double-faced spell is on the stack or a modal double-faced permanent is on the battlefield, it has only the characteristics of the face that’s up."
rule 712.8a: "While a double-faced card is outside the game or in a zone other than the battlefield or stack, it has only the characteristics of its front face."

rows.question: my buddy says once I cast a spell he can't respond until I 'pass'. I cast Lightning Bolt at his bob, do I get to keep going and cast a second Bolt before he gets a chance to counter the first one?
rows.expected_answer: Your buddy is half right. After you cast a spell you receive priority again (117.3c), so you may cast the second Bolt immediately, before he can respond to the first. He only gets priority when you pass. Nothing resolves until all players pass in succession with the stack non-empty (117.4); then only the top object resolves, and the active player gets priority again after it resolves (117.3b). So he can still respond to either Bolt once you pass, but you are entitled to stack both first.

outcome.answer:
Your buddy is right, and yes, you can chain a second Bolt before he ever gets a chance to act. When you cast a spell, the caster gets priority back afterward: "If a player has priority when they cast a spell, activate an ability, or take a special action, that player receives priority afterward" (`117.3c`). So after casting the first **Lightning Bolt**, priority returns to you, not your opponent. You can then cast a second Bolt targeting the same Bob, and priority returns to you again. Your opponent only gets priority once you actually pass. 

Once you do pass, he gets priority with two spells on the stack, and if all players pass in succession the top (most recently added) spell resolves first (`117.4`, `405.5`). So the second Bolt would resolve before the first, and he could respond to either one once he has priority, but he can't respond mid-cast to stop you from putting the second spell on the stack. Each **Lightning Bolt** deals 3 damage to any target as normal when it resolves.
citations: rule 117.3c: "If a player has priority when they cast a spell, activate an ability, or take a special action, that player receives priority afterward."
rule 117.4: "If all players pass in succession (that is, if all players pass without taking any actions in between passing), the spell or ability on top of the stack resolves"
rule 405.5: "When all players pass in succession, the top (last-added) spell or ability on the stack resolves."
oracle 4457ed35-7c10-48c8-9776-456485fdf070#0: "Lightning Bolt deals 3 damage to any target."

rows.question: I control a 2/2 with a Giant Growth resolving on it, and mid-resolution of a different spell it's technically at 0 toughness for a second (Maro-style hand-size thing). Does it die? And separately, if I have two Ragavan on the battlefield somehow, when exactly does the legend rule kick in - can I respond in between?
rows.expected_answer: 1) It doesn't die. State-based actions are only checked when a player would receive priority, not in the middle of a spell resolving (704.3, 704.4 - the CR's own Maro example). The creature only dies if it still has toughness 0 or less when SBAs are next checked (704.5f). 2) The legend rule (704.5j) is also a state-based action: the moment a player would get priority with two Ragavans you control, you choose one and the other goes to the graveyard. It doesn't use the stack and there is no window to respond between the second Ragavan entering and the legend rule applying; you can only respond before the second one enters/resolves.

outcome.answer:
No, the creature doesn't die from a mid-resolution dip to 0 toughness. State-based actions don't check anything during the resolution of a spell or ability—per `704.4`, "state-based actions pay no attention to what happens during the resolution of a spell or ability," and the rules explicitly give the Maro example: a creature that temporarily hits toughness 0 mid-resolution "will survive when state-based actions are checked" because it's back above 0 by the time the spell finishes resolving and SBAs are actually checked (which happens whenever a player would get priority, per `704.3`). So as long as your 2/2 (with Giant Growth's +3/+3 making it a 5/5) is back to positive toughness once the other spell finishes resolving, it's fine.

On the double **Ragavan**: the legend rule is a state-based action (`704.5j`), and state-based actions are performed automatically the moment they're checked, before any player receives priority (`704.3`, `117.2d` — "State-based actions happen automatically when certain conditions are met... They're dealt with before a player would receive priority"). It doesn't use the stack, isn't a triggered ability, and can't be responded to. So there's no window to "respond in between" — as soon as both Ragavans are simultaneously on the battlefield and any player would next get priority, you choose one to keep and the other goes to its owner's graveyard, with no opportunity for anyone to act first.
citations: rule 704.4: "Thus Maro will survive when state-based actions are checked."
rule 704.4: "state-based actions pay no attention to what happens during the resolution of a spell or ability"
rule 704.5j: "If two or more legendary permanents with the same name are controlled by the same player, that player chooses one of them, and the rest are put into their owners’ graveyards."

rule 704.3: "Whenever a player would get priority (see rule 117, “Timing and Priority”), the game checks for any of the listed conditions for state-based actions, then performs all applicable state-based actions s…"
rule 117.2d: "State-based actions happen automatically when certain conditions are met. See rule 704. They’re dealt with before a player would receive priority."

rows.question: my opp has [[bob]] and flipped a tim off the top, then next turn he flipped a goyf. how much life does he lose each time? goyf is like a 5/6 rn so is it 5?
rows.expected_answer: Dark Confidant makes you lose life equal to the revealed card's mana value, which is the total mana in its mana cost regardless of color (202.3). Prodigal Sorcerer costs {2}{U}, so he loses 3 life. Tarmogoyf costs {1}{G}, so he loses 2 life. Tarmogoyf's power/toughness is irrelevant; mana value is based only on the mana cost.

outcome.answer: For the **Tarmogoyf**, it's 2 life — not 5. Dark Confidant's trigger reads "reveal the top card of your library and put that card into your hand. You lose life equal to its mana value," and mana value is just the total mana in the printed mana cost (`202.3`), i.e. {1}{G} = 2. Tarmogoyf's power/toughness being 5/6 (or whatever it currently is) comes from its characteristic-defining ability — "Tarmogoyf's power is equal to the number of card types among cards in all graveyards and its toughness is equal to that number plus 1" — which only sets power and toughness, not mana cost, so it never changes the mana value Bob cares about. I don't have Tim's card text in front of me, so I can't give you the exact life loss for that flip, but whatever it is, it's likewise based on its mana cost/mana value, not its power or toughness.
